grand_strategy.reading:
Albania runs the strategy of a small state that has bet everything on being
the most useful and best-aligned partner of whoever matters, and on Edi Rama
as the man who makes that bet personal. Every relation in the card follows
from it: NATO and the American channel for security, the EU for the future,
Italy and the UK for the migration currency, the Gulf and the Kushners for
capital, Turkey for arms and religion, Kosovo for the nation. The Luttwak
pattern is that each source of leverage creates a counter-pressure that
lands on the same pillar. The EU path is only as fast as the rule of law
allows, which is the front where Rama fights his own prosecutors; the
Kosovo pact adds to Albania's security and to Serbia's rearmament; the
Trump channel brings the Board of Peace and the Sazan protests together.
In 2026 the EU front is moving (three chapters closed on 14 Jul, the
Commission calling Albania and Montenegro the closest candidates) while the
American front is cooling (the 2027 NATO summit dropped from the draft
text, 10% tariffs). Two signals that are not rows: Albania's own ministers
played down the US embassy's Iran warning of 1 Apr 2026, and Greek
diplomatic sources publicly distanced Athens from Rama's claim at Delphi
that a Hague referral was agreed. The test is whether the EU path survives
the collision between Rama's immunities draft and the benchmarks, with
Greece as a possible veto at the end.

grand_strategy.reading:
Armenia is a state that lost its war in 2020, its enclave in 2023 and its
patron's guarantee in between, and is now trying to buy a settlement and a new
set of protectors with the only coin it has left: the use of its territory. The
strategy is unusually coherent for a small state - peace with Azerbaijan first,
then a transport role (TRIPP, the Turkish rail link, Iran), then the EU and the US
as insurance, with Russia kept in the tent by gas, the base and the EAEU until the
other pieces hold. That is Luttwak's logic of the weaker party, which survives by
making itself useful to several stronger ones at once.

The paradoxes all sit at the joints. The treaty needs a constitution the June 2026
majority could not deliver; the corridor that ends the blockade is an American-run
concession through its own south; the pivot from Russia is financed by trade with
Russia; the EU law raises the cost of the gas that keeps the lights on. The
domestic fight with the Church and Karapetyan is not a side show: it is the same
contest, because the people who would vote 'no' to the preamble are also the ones
Moscow courts. Pashinyan's election win shows the public chose the pivot over the
nostalgia, but not with the margin the strategy needs, which is why the next real
test is not Moscow or Baku but a referendum with no date.

grand_strategy.reading: Austria is a middle-sized trading state that has made a security policy out of not having one, and the two things that held that bargain up - cheap Russian gas and a post-1989 buffer of friendly neighbours - are gone. The gas is gone by the company's own choice and the market's help (December 2024); the buffer is being rebuilt through the Slavkov format, the Magyar reset in Hungary, the Balkan enlargement file and a Germany that now agrees with Vienna on borders. Neutrality remains untouchable at 75% public support, so the Stocker government, squeezed by an FPÖ polling at 34-36%, does what the Cold War Austria did: it moves with the West in everything except the vocabulary (EU sanctions yes, weapons no; Sky Shield yes, NATO no; a 2% defence goal on paper and about 1.2% in the budget). The real strategic exposure is economic, not military: Germany for the market, the United States for the second-largest outlet, China for the deficit, and the Brenner for the lorries. The Russia file shows the paradox best: the espionage cases (Ott, the embassy antennas) are taken to court and the diplomats expelled, but Raiffeisen's Russian bank and its EUR 3.15bn claim keep one Austrian foot in Moscow. For the atlas, Austria is a partner of almost everyone and an ally of a few by treaty, and its grade toward each follows the structure (EU membership, trade, geography), not the declaration of neutrality.

grand_strategy.reading:
Azerbaijan runs the strategy of a state that won its central war and is
now converting a position of force into a durable order without a patron.
The 2023 recovery of Karabakh and the exodus of about 100,000 Armenians
closed the territorial question on the ground; what remains is to make
the settlement legal (the Armenian constitution, the treaty, TRIPP) and
to keep the rents that pay for it while oil declines. The method is
multi-vector balancing: a treaty alliance with Turkey, arms and oil with
Israel, jets from Pakistan, a charter with Washington, gas to Europe,
transit with China and Central Asia, and a managed truce with Russia
after the AZAL crisis. Luttwak's pattern shows in each: every success
attracts the counter-pressure that limits it. The Israeli link brought
Iranian drones, the American corridor puts Washington on Azerbaijan's
border with Armenia, the argument won against Moscow ended in a
settlement without punishment, and a regime that jails journalists is
trading the European Parliament for the European Commission. Two
signals that are not rows: Aliyev skipped the Moscow Victory Day
parade in May 2025, and in 2026 the contacts with Russia reported to
us run through a deputy prime minister and foreign ministers, with no
head-of-state meeting found; and the peace is still a text initialled
but unsigned while Azerbaijani fuel and Russian grain already cross
the old front line. The test of the next year is whether Baku lets
Armenia reach the referendum on its own terms or keeps raising the price of signing.

grand_strategy.reading:
Bulgaria's strategy is that of a small, poor, shrinking member of two clubs
that has just chosen a leader who sells distance from both while keeping the
benefits of each. The euro (1 Jan 2026), full Schengen (1 Jan 2025), the NATO
battlegroup, the F-16s and the Westinghouse fuel are the anchor and nobody in
power is seriously proposing to cut it; what moves is the margin. Rumen Radev,
elected on 19 April 2026 with a single-party majority, uses the one thing a
small state has inside the EU, the veto, on Patriarch Kirill, on Lukoil's
founder and on North Macedonia, and pays for it by leaving Ukraine's
coalition and freezing state arms aid, while the factories keep selling.
The Luttwakian pattern is plain: each gain in leverage (the veto, the special
manager at Burgas, the transit corridor, the defence industry) is bought
with a loss in trust among the same partners who guarantee the anchor, and
the paradox of the North Macedonia block shows the end of that road.
Signals that are not rows: Zakharova said on 29 May 2026 that Sofia showed
no sign of restoring dialogue with Moscow and on 14 Jul that it was 'too weak'
to help Ukraine, not turning toward Russia; the pivot is therefore toward
caution, not toward the Kremlin. The oligarch network of Peevski, Magnitsky-listed
by the US in June 2021, lost its place in government in April 2026, but the
underlying fragility (eight elections in five years, a cabinet toppled by a
budget in December 2025) has not yet been tested by a hard budget under Radev.
What to watch: the Lukoil licences (reported to run to the end of October 2026),
the 21st-package endgame, whether Skopje and Sofia talk again before the
Council's next enlargement report, and whether the 15-month BOTAS suspension
ends with a renegotiated or a litigated contract.

grand_strategy.reading:
Bosnia and Herzegovina has no single grand strategy, and a card that pretends it
has one would be wrong. The objectives above are those of the state-level
institutions as the Bosniak-led majority reads them: the Presidency member
Becirovic, the foreign minister Konakovic, the Constitutional and State Courts,
the Central Election Commission, the SDA/SDP/Troika parties. Two other agendas
sit inside the same state. The Republika Srpska leadership of Dodik's SNSD,
which has just won again, wants to hollow the state out - competences back to
the entity, the OHR gone, status defined in Washington and Moscow - and keeps
the Serb seat in the Presidency (Cvijanovic) to veto what it cannot win. The
HDZ BiH leadership of Covic, backed by Zagreb, wants an election law that stops
non-Croats from choosing the Croat member and has just obtained the seat
outright. The paradox of the whole card is that a state must defend its
existence against one of its own entities, with tools (the Bonn powers, EUFOR,
Security Council cover, the courts) that belong in part to others, in a year in
which the guarantors weakened - Schmidt resigned in May and no successor was
agreed by mid-July, the US lifted its sanctions and said it was done with
nation-building, Orban fell in April - while the electorate stayed home (42%).
Signals that are not rows: the 31 Oct 2026 Security Council vote on EUFOR (the
October 2025 renewal was 15-0, so the base case is renewal; Russia's line on the
OHR is the thing to watch), the identity of the next High Representative,
whether Hungary under Magyar keeps Orban's line toward Banja Luka, and whether
the new Presidency can still produce a majority on foreign-policy questions
after Komsic's seat goes to HDZ. Sarajevo's room for manoeuvre is real only
where the EU and the entity cannot veto it: the courts, memory politics and the
capacity to say no to Belgrade.

grand_strategy.reading:
Belarus runs the strategy of a regime that has no allies except the one that
can also swallow it. Every move is a trade of the same thin assets - territory,
prisoners, potash, nuclear hosting, the capacity to make trouble at the
border - for survival, and the Luttwak pattern is that each trade sells a part
of the autonomy it was meant to protect: protection from Russia is bought with
the right to decide on launchers and on succession, and the hybrid pressure on
Poland and Lithuania, meant to be a lever, has closed the doors Minsk wanted
to sell (transit, rail, Klaipeda). Since September 2025 Lukashenko has found a
second buyer in Trump's Washington, which pays in sanctions relief for batches
of prisoners and which neither Moscow nor Brussels can yet outbid; the question
for 2026-27 is whether the American channel (embassy, Lukashenko's possible US
trip, a potash deal) is a real exit from Moscow's orbit or only a premium on the
old rent. The evidence says the second: the Oct 2026 statements promise 'full
support' to Putin, the Oreshnik is on duty, mobilisation is under way and the
EU wall stands until February 2027. Two signals that are not rows: Lukashenko's
remark that he has 'my own understanding' of the Ukraine war (2 Oct 2026), and
the unanswered succession question - no heir has been designated, the minimum
age for the presidency was raised, and the treaty's clause on mutual support for the constitutional order gives Moscow a say
in how it will be answered.

grand_strategy.reading:
Czechia in 2026 runs two foreign policies out of one state. The government
of Andrej Babiš (ANO with the SPD and the Motorists, in office since December
2025) wants a cheaper, more domestic and more bilateral Czech Republic: no
Czech money for Ukraine, no migration pact relocation, no Green Deal, a
cautious opening to Beijing and a warm one to Jerusalem. The president, Petr
Pavel, the intelligence services and most of the arms industry keep the older
line: Russia as the threat, NATO and Berlin as the frame, Ukraine's war as
Czechia's own. Luttwak's pattern is the squeeze between them: each saving
made for the voter (the ammunition channel left unfunded, defence at 1.8%,
the opt-out from the EU loan) erodes a lever that Prague needs elsewhere -
leverage in Berlin and Washington, credibility in NATO, goodwill in Brussels
that the Dukovany loan will need before the end of 2026. What has not
changed is the structure: Russian oil and gas are out, the Korean nuclear
build is under way, Germany still takes a third of exports, and every
hostile act from Moscow (the BIS warnings, the September 2026 reciprocal
measures) pushes the cabinet back toward the line it ran against. Two signals
that are not rows: Babiš said in March 2026 that he was not planning a White
House visit and that the EU is 'always the most important'; and Pavel's
own suggestion in June 2026 that Czechia should drop the koruna for the
euro if it holds the country back, which the cabinet (which dropped the
annual euro-readiness report) will not follow.

grand_strategy.reading: Germany is a trading state that has to become a military power without having the people, the habits or the political consensus for it. Its grand strategy since 2022 is to buy security from three directions at once: from itself (the debt-brake carve-out and a Bundeswehr meant to be the strongest conventional force in Europe), from Washington (nuclear sharing, Patriot, F-35, and the hope that the troop drawdown stops at 5,000) and from a Europe it tries to organise around Paris and Warsaw. Each channel undermines another: autonomy hastens American retreat, American purchases weaken the Franco-German industrial project, spending outruns recruitment, and the domestic price, an AfD that wins eastern states while the centre governs with a thin majority, limits how much of this the electorate will fund. Its handling of Russia is the clearest part: Moscow is the declared 'greatest threat', hybrid attacks are treated as such, aid to Ukraine is the largest in Europe but stops short of Taurus and of troops. Toward China, Israel and Turkey the same Germany behaves less like a leader than like an exporter with a guilty conscience: de-risking is proclaimed and the trade deficit grows, Staatsraeson is proclaimed and then conditioned, a difficult NATO partner becomes the bet in the eastern Mediterranean. The pattern a Luttwak reader would flag is that Berlin's choices are rational one by one and self-defeating together; the test of 2027 is whether the Lithuania brigade, the F-35s and the budget become forces in being before the American drawdown and the AfD set the terms.

grand_strategy.reading: Denmark is a small state whose grand strategy has been reduced, since January 2025, to one question: how to stay in the American security system while an American president claims part of its territory. The Danish answer has three layers. Keep the formal position unmovable (sovereignty over Greenland and the Faroes, self-determination for Greenlanders), pay the price in usable goods (bases, F-35s, an Arctic build-up of tens of billions of kroner), and move the quarrel into NATO and Europe, where Rutte and the European leaders can absorb it. The 22 September 2026 trilateral agreement shows the method working and its cost: the crisis is calmer, the Kingdom's flag still flies, and both sides publish opposite readings of the same text. Behind the Greenland file stands the second pillar, which is Russia: a country that sits on the Baltic's only exit, takes the hybrid blows (drones over airports, flares at a helicopter, cables) and is both one of Ukraine's leading European donors (the Kiel tracker names it, with the Netherlands, right behind Germany for May-June 2026) and a builder of a European floor under NATO. The weakness is domestic and structural: a minority coalition, a Greenland that is no longer a colony to be spoken for, and an export economy that lives on American and German markets. The grades on this card follow the structure: the United States is a reluctant ally (a treaty ally with an open grievance, not a rival), Russia a rival (not an adversary, because Denmark seeks Moscow's restraint rather than its fall), China a reluctant partner.

grand_strategy.reading: Estonia runs the grand strategy of a front-line state that has decided to spend its way to being un-attackable rather than hope for a guarantor: 5.43% of GDP, a fortified border, a deep-strike arsenal and a dense net of partners (UK, Finland, Poland, Germany, Korea) around an American umbrella it publicly trusts and privately hedges. The Luttwak pattern is that each hardening has a cost that returns on the same front: the forward posture raises exposure, enforcement at sea shows the limits of the law, grid independence concentrates risk in cables, and the defence of the nation-state against Russian leverage on the minority hands Moscow a grievance narrative. Russia is graded a rival, not an adversary: Estonia seeks deterrence, a Russian defeat in Ukraine and a Russia that pays, not the end of the Russian state, and keeps an embassy and a border regime open. The Kremlin's line that Russia 'poses no threat' to Estonia and the Estonian intelligence judgement that Moscow has no intention of attacking in the coming year are signals, not rows: both sides are reading the other's limits. The open question for 2027 is the American presence after the end-2026 rotation and an election that a weak coalition may lose.

grand_strategy.reading:
Finland runs the strategy of a frontline state that has finally been given the
alliance it avoided for seventy years, and now has to make it real before the
patron's attention drifts. The aim is not to defeat Russia but to be an
unprofitable target: a large reserve army, American aircraft and basing,
Swedish and Nordic depth, a sealed border, and a loud insistence that Ukraine
must not lose. The grade for Russia is therefore rival, not adversary - the
government says it is not an enemy, aims at weakening Russian capacity through
sanctions and deterrence, and keeps the door open to dialogue after a ceasefire
- but the structure under it (Winter War memory, hybrid pressure, the longest
border) is hostile. The Luttwak pattern is that every layer of security adds
a new exposure: NATO membership brought instrumentalised migration, drones and
GNSS jamming; the Trump channel brought the Greenland tariff threat; the
border closure brought a Russian reply and an end to contact; the shadow-fleet
seizures ran into the law of the sea. Two signals that are not rows: Stubb's
habit of speaking both to Trump (golf, icebreakers) and of preparing Finns for
a post-war thaw with Russia, and the quiet extension of the defence memorandum
with Israel in the same years in which the president publicly condemned the
occupation. The open questions for 2027 are the election, whether the 3.2%
path survives the deficit, and whether the Eagle S case ends in a conviction
or in the Supreme Court.

grand_strategy.reading:
Georgia is run by a party that has decided its own survival, and a particular
idea of order, come before the country's formal strategy of Euro-Atlantic membership
(on paper still the constitutional line). Since the May 2024 foreign-influence law the
state has behaved as a hedging regime: it keeps every Western instrument it can without
paying the political price (candidate status, free trade, citizens' visa-free travel,
NATO contacts), keeps Russia calm (no sanctions, flights, trade, no talk of the
territories) and looks for other patrons (China, Turkey, Azerbaijan, the Gulf) and for a
different America. That is Luttwak's pattern of a move that works against its own end:
each step that protects power at home (the foreign-agents law, the arrests after
28 November 2024 and 4 October 2025, the party-ban case) lowers the value of the Western
shell that the economy rests on, and raises the weight of the one actor, Russia, whose
forces hold a fifth of the territory. Three signals that are not rows: the party ban was
widened to For Georgia in September-October 2026, a year after the first filing; Moscow
still says no dialogue without recognition of Abkhazia and South Ossetia; and a Hungarian
change of government in May 2026 reportedly removes the veto that protected Tbilisi from EU
sanctions. The Middle Corridor is the economic bet that holds the arrangement together:
cargo is up and the IMF sees 6.5% growth, but the corridor itself is not Georgia's to
secure, and its Western users are the ones being pushed away.

grand_strategy.reading:
Croatia plays the strategy of a small state that has solved its existential
question - NATO and the EU - and is now spending the dividend. Its first
objective is no longer to be admitted but to make Serbia's rearmament and
its own memory politics the neighbour's problem: it deters from inside the
Alliance, speaks to Belgrade in the voice of a member state (conditionality
on the missing, a reported weapons purchase, a defence declaration with
Tirana and Pristina) and keeps the instruments that are not its own - the
US licence on JANAF, EU loans for tanks, the High Representative in
Sarajevo - within reach. The Luttwakian pattern is that every lever is
borrowed and every success invites the response it was meant to prevent:
deterrence feeds Serbian rearmament, a refusal to receive Vucic hands him
the memorial stage, discipline on Russian oil prices out a Hungarian
partner it needs for INA. Domestically the strategy has two authors:
Plenkovic, EU-centred, tied to a Homeland Movement coalition, and
Milanovic, re-elected with 74.9%, who vetoes deployments and cancels
summits; Belgrade reads the harder voice. Two signals that are not
rows: Orban's fall in April 2026 has changed the weather with Hungary
overnight, and Serbia's snap election of 25 October 2026 may reset a tone
that Zagreb has so far refused to reset. Bosnia, where Zagreb's kin are
a constituent people dependent on imposed rules, is the arena in which
its soft power is thinnest.

grand_strategy.reading: Hungary is a mid-sized state whose grand strategy for sixteen years was to extract rents from every patron at once - Russian gas and a Rosatom reactor, Chinese factories, Gulf and Azerbaijani deals, an American president's goodwill - while using the EU veto as the currency of that bargaining. The April 2026 election replaced that model with its opposite, and the transition is the real story of the card: Magyar's Hungary wants to be a normal member of NATO and the EU (money, trust, a V4 that talks to Poland again), yet it inherits every dependency the old model built. What has changed is the tone, the people and a dozen decisions already taken - the ICC exit reversed, Russian diplomats expelled, the veto on Ukraine's clusters lifted, funds unlocked, Chinese plants inspected. What has not changed is the structure underneath: Russian crude and gas still arrive, Paks II is under review but not cancelled, the Serbian partnership and MOL's NIS deal survive the change of leader, Fico remains Hungary's closest ally in the region, the border fence stays, and the old minority grievances are only being handled differently. Luttwak's logic bites hardest on the new government: every concession to Brussels spends a lever, every audit of an Orban-era deal risks the counterpart who keeps the lights on. The next tests are dated: the Council vote on funds (13 Oct), the US waiver (21 Nov), OFAC and NIS (30 Oct), and whether Netanyahu lands in Budapest on 23 Oct.

grand_strategy.reading:
Lithuania is a small state that has chosen to be a front-line state on purpose:
it argues for the threat louder than anyone and buys the insurance before the
allies are asked to. The ranked objectives are a ladder from Russia, to the
allies' soldiers, to Ukraine, and the means mirror them - the most defence
spending in NATO relative to GDP, borrowed money from the EU to turn a brigade
into a division, and treaty exits that trade moral position for capability.
The Luttwakian friction appears wherever one rung undermines another. Border
closure and sanctions on Belarus defend the frontier but hand Minsk hostages;
leaving the mine and cluster conventions and lifting the nuclear ban deter
Moscow but enlarge Moscow's narrative; and the offer to pay for a permanent
US base binds the security of the state to a patron that is simultaneously
easing sanctions on Russian diesel and Belarusian potash. Domestic politics
adds noise, not direction: three Social Democratic cabinets in two years, a
president and a foreign minister who anchor the line on Russia, Ukraine and
Poland, and an open split on China. The Russia grade is adversary because the
Seimas calls its regime terrorist and the national assessments treat it as the
only state that can attack Lithuania; Belarus is a rival because Vilnius
aims at pressure and isolation, not at the end of the regime, and the line
softens when Washington pushes. The year to watch is 2027: the German brigade
complete, the nuclear amendment's final vote (planned 12 Jan 2027), the EU
sanctions renewal on potash, and a US rotation that may or may not become a base.

grand_strategy.reading:
Latvia is the textbook case of Luttwak's weak-state strategy: a country of 1.9
million with a long border and a large Russian-speaking population cannot win
an attritional contest with Russia, so it plays the paradoxical game of making
itself too costly to attack and too connected to be left alone. Every pillar
borrows weight from outside: the Canadian-led brigade and Article 5 for
deterrence, EU money and the escape clause for the budget, German and American
factories for the kit, Lithuania's terminal for the gas. The strategy is
consistent but its cost is dependence on partners whose own commitment is
wavering (US rotation gaps, weapons delays, the Pentagon posture review) and on
an internal politics that has shown it can fall to a single drone: the May 2026
crisis, the 52% turnout and 25% of the vote for two populist parties, one
openly pro-Russian, are the soft flank. Russia is graded adversary because the
Latvian state itself names it the existential threat and a sponsor of terrorism,
not because Riga seeks its regime's end; Belarus is a rival whose pressure is
cheap to apply and costly to stop. Two signals that are not rows: the
Silina government fell over an air-defence failure, not over foreign policy
(Kulbergs, who took over, promised to hold defence at 5% of GDP and keep a hard
line on Moscow), and part of the Russian-speaking population is still outside
the citizenry (non-citizens were 9% of residents in 2024), so the election
measures only part of the minority's weight.

grand_strategy.reading: Moldova is a state whose strategy is to turn its geography into a European fact before Russia turns it into a Russian one. PAS and Sandu hold three keys at once: a parliamentary majority renewed on 28 September 2025 despite a funded opposition, a candidate status that became real negotiations in June 2026, and a security web (EU, Romania, Ukraine, the US in Congress) that substitutes for the alliance that neutrality forbids. The central Luttwakian pattern is that every victory in the East is paid for on the Transnistrian and Gagauz flanks: cutting Gazprom and Cuciurgan freed the right bank from blackmail but ruined the left bank it hopes to reintegrate; defending elections with courts and bans hardens the audience Moscow has always had in Comrat; and tying accession to Ukraine's carries both momentum and the Hungarian veto. Two signals that are not rows: the decision to recall the ambassador from Moscow rather than expel the Russian embassy, which keeps the channel that Russia's own embassy says it wants; and Sandu's June 2026 call to put the Russian withdrawal into any Ukraine settlement, which her own foreign minister resists. Whether Moscow is an adversary is a question the ontology answers by structure: Russia's declared aim in Chișinău is a compliant government, not the end of Moldova, and Moldova's aim is a Russian departure, not Russian defeat, so the grade is rival, the hardest rival on the map.

grand_strategy.reading:
North Macedonia runs the strategy of a state that has already paid for entry
twice and now treats a third payment as a trap. It changed its name for NATO
(2018-20), accepted the French proposal for the EU (2022), and still has no date;
the Mickoski government, in office since June 2024 after winning 58 of 120 seats, draws the
conclusion that every concession reopens the account, and trades speed for
guarantees. The result is the Luttwakian pattern of a weak actor playing a long
game against two veto-holders: it keeps the one thing it has already won (NATO,
near-total alignment with Brussels on Russia and Ukraine) and widens its list of
patrons, with Washington, Ankara and, until Orban's fall, Budapest and Belgrade
behind it. The price is a country neither inside nor outside the EU, and a
population that votes with its feet. Two signals that are not rows: the
Commission's report of November 2025 states flatly that 'no attempts were made' to
adopt the amendments, while von der Leyen's visit of 2 October 2026 produced the
first agreed step in years, so the next weeks (the foreign minister's trip to Sofia
during a Corridor 8 event) are the test of whether the 'stronger pressure' Mickoski
awaits has arrived. Open gaps: no source was found on Russian influence on the
2024 vote, on Chinese projects under this government, or on any Greek retaliation
after 2024.

grand_strategy.reading: Montenegro runs the grand strategy of a twenty-year-old micro-state that has bet its survival on being absorbed into the institutions that guarantee small states: NATO (done in 2017) and the EU (the 2028 target). The method is alignment as proof - full CFSP alignment, expulsions of Russian operatives, a defence budget above 2% - and the resource is speed: it is the only candidate with 18 chapters closed. The Luttwakian trap is that the last chapters are not technical. Croatia's veto turns on wartime grievances from the 1990s, and the Spajic majority rests on parties that treat the 2006 independence as a wound, so every step that pleases Belgrade's friends at home (the Jasenovac resolution, the Mladic condolences) costs a vote in Zagreb or The Hague, while every step toward Brussels costs the coalition's Serbian flank. The same logic runs through the economy: the Gulf and Turkish capital that replaces Chinese debt arrives with procedure-bypassing laws that the Commission itself flags. Two signals that are not rows: the cadence of closures (December 2025, January, March, June and July 2026) and President Milatovic's repeated returns of laws to Parliament, a veto that keeps the Constitutional Court and Brussels in the loop. With the Serbian election on 25 Oct 2026 and Montenegro's own on June 2027, the question is whether the accession treaty can be finished before the identity politics of one of the two neighbours changes the arithmetic.

grand_strategy.reading: Norway runs the strategy of a rich small state on the edge of a hostile great power: its security is borrowed from the Atlantic alliance, its wealth comes from the thing Europe needs most, and both are now wielded under pressure. Since 2022 it has turned its income into the three things it can use: gas for Europe's grid, the Nansen programme for Ukraine, and a defence budget heading for 3.5% of GDP. The classic Luttwakian pattern is that each lever works against the next: gas and the fund make Norway central and rich, but also a target and, for Washington, an object to press (tariffs, the fund's ethics, the Greenland episode). In response it is pluralising its guarantors (UK frigates and Lunna House, German submarines, the EU defence partnership, Nordic integration with Sweden and Finland), while remaining dependent on US aircraft and US reinforcement. With Russia the policy is firm and unromantic: sanctions, public naming of GPS jamming and espionage, but also a fisheries regime and a Svalbard Treaty that Oslo wants to keep working. The seizure of the Professor Molchanov on 2 Sep 2026 shows the limits of that dual policy; it will be tested next by the Russian appeal and by how far Moscow pushes Svalbard. Domestically the Støre minority government depends on left parties whose priorities (oil phase-out, divestment from Israel) cut across the fund and the energy exports that give Norway its influence; the 2027 budget will test it again. Two signals that are not rows: Norway refused a seat on the Board of Peace on principle, and its Arctic Council chairship ended in May 2025 with Russia still excluded from political dialogue, so the forum Norway invested in is now under Danish-Greenlandic stewardship in the middle of the Greenland dispute. Gaps: the rate of the US tariff now in force, the US Marine rotation (only prepositioning and exercises are sourced), the 2024-25 restrictions on Chinese investment (no source found; only Security Act screening, the Telenor-Huawei decision of 2019 and the 2026 threat assessments are documented), and the US share of the fund's equity.

grand_strategy.reading: Poland is a frontline state that has turned geography into rank: it spends the most in NATO, hosts about 10,000 US troops and the logistics hub of the Ukraine war, and treats Russia not as a rival but as the standing threat. Its grand strategy is a double reinsurance. The Atlantic leg (American troops, F-35s, Patriot, hopes of a permanent base and of nuclear sharing) is run mostly by President Nawrocki; the European leg (SAFE money, the German pact, French deterrence talks, a revived Visegrad) is run by Tusk's government. They are complementary on paper and rivalrous in practice, and the Luttwak logic bites exactly there: the more Warsaw tries to be everyone's indispensable ally, the more each guarantor discounts a promise that two offices make differently. The same logic runs through its neighbours. Poland needs Ukraine standing but taxes it with grain bans and Volhynia; it needs Germany but keeps a reparations claim; it seals the Belarus border and in doing so cuts the Chinese rail traffic that crosses it. The grade of Russia is 'adversary' rather than 'rival' because Warsaw's own officials call Russian sabotage state terrorism and Russia the main threat to Poland and Central Europe, and because the Kremlin itself says relations have 'deteriorated completely'; against that, Poland has no aim of regime change in Russia, which is why the grade carries confidence B and not A. Ukraine is a 'reluctant ally' - indispensable, aligned by necessity, with an open historical wound - and Belarus a 'rival' that is warming only because Washington brokered a prisoner swap. The central uncertainty is what Poland is in 2027: a country whose security depends on a US president's mood, or one that has bought, built and borrowed enough to depend on itself.

grand_strategy.reading: Romania is a frontline state with a rear-area politics. Its grand strategy is borrowed security: bind the United States, NATO and the EU to the Black Sea by hosting their bases, buying their arms with their loans and keeping Ukraine and Moldova alive as buffers. The method has worked in hardware (Kogalniceanu, Deveselu, F-35s, SAFE) and fails at the margin Washington controls: the brigade left in October 2025 while Bucharest was offering a base for the Iran operation five months later. What is new in 2026 is that the weak point is internal. The annulled election of 2024 did not remove the sovereigntist vote, a third of Parliament, and the fiscal repair that the EU and the rating agencies demanded took the coalition apart; the country has had a caretaker cabinet since 5 May and a fourth nominee since 5 October, with every agency one step above junk. Neighbours show the same split between kinship and interest: Moldova is kin and a partner, Ukraine is a partner and a dispute over Romanian schools, Hungary is a co-member whose new government (Magyar, April 2026) has restarted the conversation, Serbia is a partner it presses on the Vlachs, Turkey the one NATO ally in the Black Sea with ships and a strategic partnership. China is held at arm's length by law (the 5G rules that exclude Huawei) and, since Dan's remarks on the 2025 strategy, with open caution; Israel is a partner whose war Romania abstained on in 2023 and 2024 and voted for the Palestinian seat in 2026. Read through Luttwak, the danger is that Romania's policy of making itself useful rests on stable government in Bucharest, which is the thing it lacks.

grand_strategy.reading:
Serbia runs a hedging strategy with one fixed point - Kosovo - and everything else
negotiable. In Luttwak's terms the paradox is structural: the instrument that
protects the fixed point (Russian and Chinese cover at the UN) is the one that
blocks the declared strategic goal (EU membership), and the "neutrality" that
justifies the hedge is financed by the side the hedge is meant to keep at a
distance. Through 2025-26 the hedge stopped paying: the US sanctioned NIS, Russia
refused a long-term gas contract and accused Belgrade over ammunition, the EU
froze funds and talks after the Mladić funeral. Two signals worth watching that
are not rows: Vučić did not attend the 2026 Moscow parade, and in May 2026 Serbia
held its first-ever exercise with NATO on its own soil. The 25 Oct 2026 election
decides whether the strategy has an author at all.

grand_strategy.reading:
Slovakia is the case of a small, trade-dependent member state that uses
the rules of the club it belongs to as its main instrument against the
club. Fico has no army to speak of, no oil, and an export economy
wired into German supply chains; what he has is unanimity. The 2023-26
pattern is therefore linkage: a veto (the 18th and 20th sanctions
packages, Ukraine's loan, the accession clusters) is held until a
concrete good is released - gas guarantees, Druzhba oil, a hearing. That
is Luttwak's paradoxical logic in a small space: the weaker the state,
the more it relies on the one resource, procedure, that its partners
cannot take away without breaking their own rules. But the lever
consumes itself. Hungary under Orban was the other half of the veto
axis; after Magyar's win in April 2026 Bratislava is alone, the
Parliament has asked for conditionality, and the Visegrad revival is
being run by Tusk, Babis and Magyar, not by Fico. Two signals that are
not rows: Fico took the Moscow trip again in May 2026 after having
been shot in 2024 and after a year of mass protest, which shows that
the trips are a message to a domestic electorate and not a
diplomatic programme (OSW and others make this reading of the
American hardware too); and on 18 Sep 2026 he said he would not
be 'part of any military conflict because of Article 5' - a statement
that, if believed, hollows out the alliance whose F-16s he is flying.
The coalition crisis of September 2026 may end the story before the
2027 election: the structural question is whether his successor,
whoever it is, will inherit a state that has learned to veto or one
that has learned to be vetoed.

grand_strategy.reading:
Slovenia is a small, rich, open economy whose strategy is to stay inside every
club (EU, euro, Schengen, NATO) and to spend as little as possible on anything
that is not membership. Its distinctive feature in 2022-26 is that the content
of foreign policy swings with the government while the anchors do not move:
Golob's Slovenia used the Security Council seat to be the EU's most outspoken
critic of Israel; Janša's Slovenia, since June 2026, pays its dues to NATO,
courts Trump and reopens to Israel. One signal that is not a row: Israel's
announced embassy in Ljubljana, the visible reward for the reversal.
What this card could not source and leaves open: Ukraine aid, Western Balkans
advocacy, China, Italy, Trieste and Koper, tariffs and the Hungarian media loan.

grand_strategy.reading: Sweden after 2022 runs the strategy of a small, rich, technologically capable state that has given up the protection of neutrality for the protection of numbers, and is spending to make the swap pay. The organising idea is the Baltic as a NATO lake: Finland, Poland and Denmark are treated as one theatre, the Gripen, the A26 and the CV90 are the instruments of alignment as much as of defence, and the United States is kept inside the system by treaty (the DCA) while Europe is built up for the day it steps back. The Luttwakian pattern is that every step that raises Sweden's value to the alliance also raises its exposure and its bills (the front-line host, the donated Gripens, the loans behind 3.5%), and that the bargains that bought the membership (Turkey, Hungary) taught others that a veto has a price. Two signals are not rows. First, the 13 September 2026 vote ended the Tidö era without producing a successor: the next government will probably keep NATO, Ukraine and the 3.5% target (all large Riksdag majorities) but will change the Israel line and perhaps the EU budget posture, so the card's stability is higher on security than on foreign economic policy. Second, the brief's 'Ukraine 100-year partnership' is not in the record: Sweden's agreement with Ukraine is a ten-year security agreement of May 2024; a 100-year format belongs to the United Kingdom. The Kurdish question behind the accession has faded from the news but not from the memorandum Ankara still holds.

grand_strategy.reading:
Türkiye runs the grand strategy of a middle power that has decided to be a hinge
rather than a bloc member: it keeps the second-largest army in NATO and hosts its
2026 summit, buys Russian gas and an S-400, signs a mutual-defence pact with
Riyadh and Islamabad, and offers itself as the venue and mediator that every
side needs. The currency is indispensability, and it works because nobody can
afford to push Ankara out. Luttwak's pattern appears at each seam: the S-400 that
proved autonomy cost the F-35; the victory in Syria draws Israeli bombs on its
airbase; the Blue Homeland decrees imperil the customs union; the boycott of
Israel closes the Gaza seat. Underneath sits regime security. The two things the
leadership most needs in 2026 - the end of the PKK war (Law 7595, the SDF's
dissolution) and a path to keep power (the İmamoğlu trial) - are domestic
before they are foreign, and they set the tone of the external line: a
'Terror-Free Türkiye' that justifies Syrian and Iraqi policy, and a Western
reconciliation (Trump's promise of sanctions relief and the F-35) pursued
without conditions on rule of law. Signals that are not rows: Ankara has not
joined Western sanctions on Russia and cut Russian crude only after Trump's
appeal of Sept 2025; Washington's envoy to Syria is also its ambassador in
Ankara, which makes Turkey the channel for US policy in Damascus. The open
questions for the next quarter are whether Trump's promise becomes a legal
instrument, whether the Blue Homeland law passes in October, and whether the
Israel-Turkey deconfliction mechanism in Syria is built before the next strike.

grand_strategy.reading:
Ukraine runs a grand strategy of the weaker party that must make itself
indispensable to stronger ones: it cannot win the war outright, cannot
afford to lose it, and has to keep three patrons (the EU, the UK-led
coalition, the United States) paying while it negotiates with an adversary
whose price is its statehood. At the tactical level it is holding (the
front is slow in 2026, drones and strikes compensate for men), at the
theatre level it is trading minerals, drones and the promise of a rebuilt
country for money and guarantees, and at the grand-strategic level it is
betting that the road to the EU gives it an anchor that no ceasefire can
cancel. Luttwak's reversal is everywhere: the same logic that keeps the
patrons engaged (usefulness, visible strength, deep strikes, a national
story told in battle) irritates the neighbours whose vetoes decide the
anchor, from Fico's pipeline to Warsaw's history. 2026 is also the year the
centre of the question moved from the front to the table: talks opened
in Abu Dhabi in January, were frozen by the Iran war in March, and resumed
with the Miami round of 9-10 October, while the Kremlin still demands the
Donbas. Two signals that are not rows: the new Hungarian government's
shift from veto to conditions (Magyar, since May) and the Ankara
summit's quiet re-labelling of Ukraine as a contributor to Euro-Atlantic
security. Open question for the next review: whether the 15 Oct European
Council and the Miami outcome change the guarantee from a text to a force.

grand_strategy.reading:
Kosovo runs the strategy of a state that exists on the ground and not yet in
law: every move is a bid to turn effective control into recognised status, and
the only currencies it has are loyalty and usefulness to the West. That
produces the central Luttwakian pattern: the actions that prove statehood
(mayors in the north, the army, rail stations, the war-memory law) are the
ones that cost it the patrons who could confer it, while the actions that would
please the patrons (the Community of Serb-majority Municipalities, Serbian
return to the judiciary) are those it fears would hollow out statehood from
within. Since 2025 the pressure has eased on one flank (EU measures lifted in
March 2026, institutions completed in September-October) and tightened on
another (KFOR shrinking, a cooler Washington, the Specialist Chambers
verdicts). Two signals that are not rows: the US launched a strategic dialogue with
Belgrade on 17 July 2026 although Kosovo had joined the Board of Peace and
pledged troops to Gaza, and the 6 Oct law on the Hague court was passed under
street pressure, not diplomatic calculation. With
the 25 Oct Serbian election ahead, Pristina's real question is whether the
stalled Ohrid road can be re-opened by a new government in Belgrade.

ARM.note: Until 2023 the pair was the ontology's reference case of 'adversary'. Since the loss of Nagorno-Karabakh (offensive of 19-20 Sep 2023, more than 100,000 people fled in ten days) Yerevan has accepted Baku's terms: treaty text agreed 13 Mar 2025, initialled in Washington on 8 Aug 2025, Minsk Group dissolved on 1 Sep 2025, transit ban lifted 21 Oct 2025, Pashinyan saying in October 2026 that 'peace is established'. Not 'partner' because the treaty is unsigned and conditional on a constitutional referendum, 19 Armenians are in Baku's prisons (Vardanyan, 20 years, Feb 2026), the Shaki shooting of Oct 2026 is open, and the Armenian opposition calls the preamble demand imposed by Baku. Not 'adversary' because Armenia seeks recognition of borders, not Azerbaijan's defeat. Asymmetry risk: Baku is likely to grade Armenia lower than 'rival' warming; its card is not yet written. Serbia's card grades Azerbaijan 'partner' (strategic partners, defence contract, gas); it holds nothing on Armenia, so there was nothing to mirror for this pair.

ARM.note: Russia is still Armenia's treaty ally on paper (CSTO membership, which the dataset turns into an 'ally' floor; the 1997 friendship treaty; the 102nd base in Gyumri, lease to 2044) and its largest trading partner (35.5% of foreign trade), gas monopolist and remittance source. In structure it is no longer an alliance: the CSTO has been frozen since February 2024, Pashinyan says Armenia will not return in the next five years and that he would be 'very pleased' to be expelled, Russian border guards left Zvartnots on 31 Jul 2024, Russia's share of arms procurement fell from over 96% to about 10%, Pashinyan says 'we are not Russia's allies on Ukraine' and that the Gyumri base 'adds nothing', and Moscow answers with import bans (spring 2026), a notified threat to denounce the gas agreement (27 May 2026) and Medvedev's 'second Ukraine' (Oct 2026). Carnegie reports Putin now deals with Pashinyan 'as a partner, albeit a problematic one, not as an ally'. Hence 'partner' (transactional, unaligned) rather than 'reluctant_ally' or 'rival'. Bond - grievance: the lasting wound is Russia's non-intervention in 2021-23 and the Karabakh loss, laid on top of deep economic and human ties (a large diaspora and workers in Russia). Armenia is not Russia's mortal enemy and Russia is not Armenia's.

AUT.note: Not an adversary: Austria wants no change of regime in Moscow, stays neutral in the military sense and kept the Gazprom contract until OMV ended it itself. But it backs every EU sanctions package, sends Ukraine non-military aid, convicted Egisto Ott for espionage for Moscow (May 2026) and expelled three Russian diplomats on 4 May 2026 over an antenna array on embassy roofs, bringing the total to 14 since 2020; the foreign minister called the abuse of diplomatic immunity 'unacceptable'. Cooling because the gas break (16 Nov 2024) removed the last big material tie and the espionage cases keep coming; the Raiffeisen bank and the EUR 3.15bn Rasperia claim are the remaining entanglement. The FPÖ (first in 2024) wants an end to sanctions, so the line depends on the coalition. Bond - none: an interest-only relation since the 1955 State Treaty ended the occupation.

AZE.note: Until 2023 the pair were mortal enemies (the ontology's reference case for 'adversary'). Since the Karabakh offensive of 19-20 Sep 2023 and the exodus of about 100,000 Armenians, Baku's aim is no longer Armenia's defeat but a settlement on its terms: the treaty was initialled in Washington on 8 Aug 2025, transit restrictions were lifted on 21 Oct 2025 and fuel exports to Armenia run at USD 17.6m in January-August 2026. Still not a partner: the constitution is a precondition for signing, 'Western Azerbaijan' is in official use, Armenian churches are being demolished and the Karabakh leaders were sentenced in February 2026 (Vardanyan 20 years). Warming because of the Washington text, the transit and the June 2026 Armenian election, which left Civil Contract short of a constitutional majority.

BGR.note: No source calls the relationship 'rival'; the grade is our reading of the structure (confidence C). Bulgaria is a NATO and EU member that expelled Russian diplomats in 2020-22, put Lukoil's Bulgarian subsidiaries under a state special manager under US sanctions (Nov 2025), is moving Kozloduy off Russian fuel and carries Russian gas only as a transit state; Zakharova said on 29 May 2026 that Sofia showed 'no sign' of restoring dialogue. Not 'adversary': nothing in Sofia's stated aim is Russia's defeat, Radev wants 'pragmatic' relations and blocked the Kirill and Alekperov listings. Not 'neutral': it is inside the sanctions regime and the NATO frontline. Trend stable: the Radev line softens tone and sanctions votes without changing the structure, and Moscow itself reads Sofia as 'too weak', not turning. Bond - kin: Slavic and Orthodox ties, the 1878 liberation narrative and the Russophile electorate (Vazrazhdane 12 seats, BSP) that make a clean break impossible.

EST.note: Rival, not adversary: Estonia's aim is deterrence, a Russian defeat in Ukraine and payment of damages, not the end of the Russian state or its regime; it keeps a border regime and diplomatic contact (chargé d'affaires summoned). The friction is the sharpest in the Baltic: MiG-31 intrusion and Article 4 request (19 Sep 2025), the Jaguar/Su-35 episode (May 2025), GPS jamming, the Milrem arson blamed on Russian services (Sep 2026), the Estlink 2 cut. Estonian foreign intelligence calls Russia the main threat but judges it has no intention to attack in the coming year; the Kremlin says it poses no threat to Estonia. No source uses 'rival': the grade is our reading of the structure (confidence C), and Moscow's side (RUS card) is expected to grade Estonia more harshly - an asymmetric pair that is deliberate. Bond - grievance: the Soviet occupation and Russian claim to protect Russian speakers.

EST.note: Treaty ally under NATO Article 5 with a rotational US presence of over 600 troops; but the trend is cooling. The Pentagon cancelled the Poland-bound rotation from which part of the US contingent in Estonia was to come (5,000-troop drawdown, May 2026), Estonian public trust in Trump is low, and the future of the US presence after the rotation ending in 2026 is under review, while Pevkur says he trusts the US and does not expect withdrawal. Friction is about the commitment, not the structure, so ally and not reluctant ally. Bond - affinity: US non-recognition of the Soviet annexation and 30 years of security partnership.

FIN.note: Why rival and not adversary: Finland's own line is that Russia is not an enemy but its actions and breaches of international law are opposed (Valtonen, April 2025), and the declared strategy is to support Ukraine, weaken Russia through sanctions and strengthen defence - deterrence and containment, not an aim of Russia's defeat or regime. Yet the Government Defence Report (Dec 2024) calls Russia a long-term threat that will outlast the war, Supo names it the main threat, the eastern border has been shut since December 2023, Russia closed five rail crossings on 1 Jul 2026, and Peskov says Finland and Sweden 'reduced relations to zero'. Stubb (31 Mar 2025) says Finns must prepare mentally for an eventual thaw, so the door is not closed. Bond - grievance: Winter War memory and the 1,340 km border, now sharpened by hybrid pressure (instrumentalised migration, GNSS jamming, cable incidents). Our reading of the grade is C-level on the word itself; the structure is documented by tier 1 sources.

FIN.note: Member since 4 April 2023 (Article 5). The alliance is the centre of Finnish strategy; the NATO land command in Mikkeli is operational (1 Sep 2025), Forward Land Forces Finland stood up on 6 Jun 2026, and Stubb led the delegation to the Ankara summit (7-8 Jul 2026). Friction is minimal and is aimed at members (US tariffs) rather than at the alliance. Bond - affinity: Finns chose membership after seventy years of non-alignment; support is above 70%.

FIN.note: The treaty ally and patron: NATO Article 5, the DCA (15 sites, in force 1 Sep 2024, passed by Parliament unanimously), the F-35 (64 aircraft), the Arctic cutter deal signed by Trump and Stubb on 9 Oct 2025. There is visible friction - the January 2026 tariff threat over Greenland, the 15% US tariff on EU goods - which is why the trend is not warming; Stubb calls Greenland the hardest issue for Finland. The presidential channel to Trump is personal (golf, Mar-a-Lago, the White House) and is the reason the grade holds. Bond - affinity: no historical kinship, but a strong sympathy and a security bet that Finland has no alternative to.

FIN.note: Member since 1995 (EU Article 42(7) mutual assistance clause). The Orpo government is a pro-security, anti-debt member: it rejects a 2028-34 budget near EUR 2 trillion and any common-debt instrument, insists on conditionality, and joins the net-contributor group, yet pushes the EU hardest on Ukraine finance and the use of immobilised Russian assets. That is friction on the price, not on the structure, so it stays ally and not reluctant ally. The migration policy of the coalition (stricter asylum, time-limited protection) is national. Bond - affinity: the EU is the economic anchor and the second security layer.

FIN.note: Pragmatic and narrowing. Finland follows the EU formula of cooperation, competition and systemic rivalry; it blocked Chinese purchases on security grounds, and the 2025-29 action plan agreed on Stubb's state visit (Oct 2024) is leaner and avoids the Arctic. China is the third source of Finnish imports (9.4%) and fifth export market (4.5%, the lowest since 2009). The Newnew Polar Bear dragged its anchor over the Balticconnector (8 Oct 2023); China called it a storm accident, and the captain is on trial in Hong Kong. Wang Yi met Stubb in Turku on 5 Jul 2026 and Valtonen in Helsinki, with talk of more exchanges. A source using the word partner is the Chinese readout; the grade is our reading of the structure (hence C). Bond - none.

GEO.note: Claimed, not controlled: Russia and the local authorities hold Abkhazia since the 1992-93 war and Moscow's 2008 recognition; Tbilisi does not recognise it and calls it occupied, and Western governments repeat the 20%-occupied figure. The claim is frozen (no force, no policy to retake it). Direct Moscow-Sukhumi flights resumed in May 2025 over Georgian protests; a Russian-built customs terminal in Gali was reported in December 2025 and Kobakhidze denied Georgian involvement. Bond grievance: the 1992-93 war and its displacement. Mirrors the objective row.

GEO.note: Structural reading, not rhetoric: Russia occupies 20% of Georgia's territory and there are no diplomatic relations since 2008, so 'partner' is excluded even though Georgian Dream has warmed trade, flights, tourism and tone (Ashgabat, December 2025; Kobakhidze, August 2026, defending the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk and calling sanctions a 'second front'). Not 'adversary': the government does not aim at Russia's defeat or regime and says restoration of ties is impossible only while the territories' status is unchanged. Moscow's own line (3 December 2025): no grounds for political dialogue without recognition. Jamestown calls the direction a drift 'back into Russia's orbit'; no source uses the grade word (confidence C). Bond grievance: 2008 and the occupation. Warming is the government's trajectory, not the public's.

GEO.note: Cooperates out of necessity while resisting alignment: the EU is the free-trade and visa-free anchor and candidate status was granted in December 2023, but since the 2024 foreign-influence law Tbilisi rejects the EU's conditions, refuses sanctions on Russia and called the November 2024 suspension of accession talks (until the end of 2028) a choice. The Commission now calls Georgia a candidate 'in name only', has downgraded political contacts, suspended assistance benefiting the authorities and suspended visa-free travel for diplomatic and service passports (6 March 2026). Not 'partner' in the plain sense (the government keeps the stated goal of membership by 2030 while the Commission says the process is at a standstill) and not 'rival' because the EU remains Georgia's institutional shell. No source uses the grade word (C). Bond affinity: the constitutional aim and a pro-European public. Cooling: Hungary, the main shield against EU sanctions, changed government in May 2026.

HRV.note: Mirrors Serbia's own reading (SRB toward HRV: rival, cooling, grievance) with the same sources, and adds Zagreb's side. Not 'adversary': Croatian officials say they do not form a military alliance against Serbia and do not expect it to use the new Chinese missiles against neighbours (Plenkovic, March 2026), while the Human Security Centre puts the war risk 'very low' but the tension real. Friction is sharp and rising: Serbian diplomat expulsions and reciprocal moves (Nov 2023), Belgrade's ambassador recalled after the 18 Mar 2025 Tirana declaration, Vucic's 'greatest threat' line (Munich 2026), Plenkovic writing to NATO about Serbia's CM-400AKG missiles (Mar 2026), Milanovic cancelling the Brdo-Brijuni summit (30 Mar 2026), 1,725 missing persons with no archive cooperation. Croatia is also the sole crude route for Serbia (JANAF), which makes the pair interdependent. Bond - grievance: the 1991-95 war, Vukovar and Jasenovac as memory.

Bosnia is Croatia's largest non-EU export market (10.8%). Partner, not ally: no alignment treaty, and Zagreb's priorities for Croats sit uneasily with a Bosniak-led reading of the state. Bond - kin: the Croats of Bosnia, about whom HDZ BiH and HDZ coordinate.

Slovenia's new government under Janez Jansa (confirmed 22 May 2026) is right-of-centre but no 2026 statement on the border was found. HRV.note: NATO and EU co-member, tied by oil: JANAF carries non-Russian crude to MOL, Hungarian firms hold Krk LNG capacity, and Hungary supplied EUR 3.2bn (7.1%) of Croatia's imports in 2025. Warming because Peter Magyar, who won the April 2026 election, told Plenkovic at Bled on 31 Aug 2026 he was ready for 'a new chapter' on INA and the two directed their foreign and economy ministers to talk. Reluctant ally rather than partner because both are bound by treaty (NATO, EU) but the business is adversarial. Bond none: interest only.

HUN.note: Member since 2004, so the 'partner' grade of non-members does not apply; the co-member rule gives reluctant_ally while friction remains. Sixteen years of vetoes and Article 7 ended with the 12 Apr 2026 election (Tisza 53%, 138 of 199 seats; 'the Hungarian people have said yes to Europe'). The Commission proposed on 23 Sep 2026 to release EUR 4.2bn of the funds frozen since 2022 and the Council meets on 13 Oct; EUR 3.5bn is still blocked over the child-protection, academic-freedom and asylum files, and Hungary's court case against the EU's Russian gas ban and the migration-pact fight show the friction is not over. Bond affinity: a government that wants to be inside, not a rebel.

Humanitarian aid but no weapons for Ukraine. Hungary has 410 troops in KFOR.

HUN.note: NATO ally, so not 'partner'. Washington was Orban's patron: Vance campaigned for him days before the vote, Trump gave him a one-year waiver on Russian oil and gas sanctions and an open-ended one for Paks II in Nov 2025 against US LNG and nuclear-fuel purchases. After the vote Trump called Magyar 'a good man' and the US embassy promised close cooperation, but no White House invitation is reported, a pro-Fidesz outlet describes a missed handshake at the Ankara summit, and the waiver lapses on 21 Nov 2026 with Budapest asking for an extension. The 'cooling' is a reading of lost patronage, not a US act (confidence C). Bond affinity: the Biden-era freeze is over and migration politics still overlaps.

HUN.note: EU member against a candidate: a rival, not a reluctant ally. Hungary held the accession veto for 17 months, withheld clusters 2 and 3 on 17 Jul, 1 Sep and 8 Sep 2026 and still opposes a fast-track and gives no weapons. Not adversary: Budapest never wished Ukraine's defeat. No source uses the word rival (confidence C). Bond grievance: the minority question; Kyiv grades Hungary the same way (rival, warming, grievance).

HUN.note: Treaty-based strategic partnership (2021) with a defence agreement (2023, implementing agreement 2025) that Belgrade reads as an alliance and Telex calls 'a far cry from' one; Serbia grades Hungary 'ally'. The structural facts: Serbian TurkStream gas passes to Hungary, MOL is buying Gazprom Neft's 56.15% of NIS, the Chinese-built Budapest-Belgrade railway is delayed, and Vojvodina's Hungarians keep Budapest attached. After 12 Apr 2026 the tone is cordial at government level (Vucic phone call, July ambassador farewell) but Magyar hinted Vucic's 'godfather' relationship with Orban and Fico, and Vucic retorted that Serbia is not Magyar's country. Cooling because the personal patron is gone. Bond affinity: Vojvodina's minority and the shared sovereigntist camp.

HUN.note: The remaining ally of the Orban years: Fico and Orban shared the Druzhba line, the lawsuit against the EU ban on Russian gas and the vetoes on Ukraine. LTU.note: Review 2026-10-12: regraded from adversary to rival for consistency with Estonia, Latvia-to-be and Poland; 'adversary' is reserved for actors seeking each other's destruction (Iran-Israel), while Lithuania seeks deterrence and a Russian defeat in Ukraine, not the end of the Russian state. The Seimas 'terrorist state' resolutions are the hardest rhetoric in NATO but the structural position is the same as its Baltic neighbours'. Reserved for mortal enemies, and the evidence is a declared view of Russia's regime, not rhetoric: the Seimas voted in May 2022 that Russia supports and perpetrates terrorism, and in March 2023 asked the world to recognise it as a terrorist state; the 2026 national threat assessment treats Russia as the primary threat and dates a limited Baltic war to 3-5 years after a Ukraine ceasefire. Hostile action is documented on Lithuanian soil (IKEA arson sentenced Nov 2025, 36 GPS-spoofing antennas in Kaliningrad). Lithuania does not seek Russia's disappearance, which is why this is the edge of the grade; the Russian regime's behaviour is the problem, and it backs Ukraine's victory by law (0.25% of GDP). Cooling: 'cooling' here means hardening. Residual commerce (Kaliningrad gas transit to 2030) is a legal obligation, not a bond. Bond - grievance: the 1940-91 occupation. The reciprocal Russian stance has not been written.

LVA.note: Review 2026-10-12: regraded from adversary to rival for consistency with Estonia and Lithuania; 'adversary' is reserved for actors seeking each other's destruction (Iran-Israel). The Saeima's 'state sponsor of terrorism' declaration and the chargé-level relations are the hardest posture in NATO, but Riga's aim is deterrence and a Russian defeat in Ukraine, not the end of the Russian state. The Latvian state itself uses the vocabulary of the mortal enemy: the State Security Service (VDD) puts Russia's services at the head of the threats to the state and a secondary account of its February 2026 report calls Russia an existential threat; the Saeima declared Russia a state sponsor of terrorism on 11 Aug 2022 (67 votes, none against); relations were cut to charge d'affaires level on 24 Feb 2023; and Latvian soil has seen Russian-directed arson cells (cases of 2023-25), GPS jamming from Kaliningrad, and Russian rail crossings shut from 1 Jul 2026. Adversary rather than rival because the declared Latvian aim is Russia's defeat in Ukraine and the Russian state is named the threat to Latvia's existence, not a competitor. The case against: Riga seeks no change of regime in Moscow, keeps an embassy, and still sold EUR 962.5m of goods to Russia in 2025 (4.9% of exports), so the grade is the harder of two readings (the 'rival' reading is the fallback). Bond - grievance: the 1940 occupation and the Soviet deportations, and more than a third of residents who are not ethnic Latvians, mostly Russian-speaking.

Moldova's aim is withdrawal of the Russian garrison and a stop to interference, not Russia's defeat; embassies remain open and Russia's own embassy (11 Aug 2026) says it is open to dialogue; Russia's aim in Chișinău is a compliant government, not the abolition of the state. The structure is the hardest rival, not an adversary. No source uses the word 'rival': the grade is our reading (confidence C). Bond - grievance: 1992 war, a 30-year occupation, subversion.

ROU.note: The 2025-2030 National Defence Strategy puts Russia's hybrid war and its aggression against Ukraine first among the threats, Moscow's drones have crossed, hit (Galati, 29 May 2026) and been shot down over Romania, and the two have traded consul and diplomat expulsions since 29 May 2026 (Constanta consulate closed; St Petersburg consulate closed 25 Jun; embassy official expelled and ambassador recalled 27 Jul). It stays rival, not adversary: no Romanian source states an aim of Russia's defeat or regime change, and the ontology keeps adversary for mortal enemies (Ukraine's grade toward Russia). Cooling because the incidents are now physical and the diplomatic channel is thinning. Bond - grievance: the Soviet legacy in Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina and the Dec 2024 election interference.

TUR.note: NATO co-member with visible friction, so reluctant_ally (not a plain ally). The grievance is structural: the F-35 expulsion of 2019, CAATSA sanctions of December 2020 and Washington's past support for the Syrian Kurds. The trend is warming under Trump: Erdogan was received at the White House on 25 Sep 2025 (and cut Russian crude after Trump's appeal), Trump said in Ankara on 7 Jul 2026 'we're going to be taking the sanctions off', Erdogan says he got 'a promise' on the F-35, and on 2 Oct Trump still gave no timetable. The legal barrier (congressionally mandated sanctions, the S-400 still in Turkey) is why this is a promise and not yet a change of structure. Bond - grievance.

TUR.note: Transactional partner and not an ally: Turkey is in NATO and has backed Ukraine's sovereignty, but has not joined Western sanctions, kept the straits closed to warships of both sides under Montreux (Feb 2022), brokered the Black Sea Grain Initiative (22 Jul 2022 - Russia left in Jul 2023) and keeps the S-400 (2019), 22 bcm a year of Gazprom contracts (extended Dec 2025), Russia as largest petroleum supplier (47.5% in Dec 2025, down from 61.1% in Oct) and the Akkuyu plant (first unit due end of 2026). Erdogan told Putin in Bishkek on 1 Sep 2026 that relations are at 'the highest level'. Stable because the dependence is mutual and Ankara is trimming oil, not gas. Syria and Libya are now mutual deconfliction rather than rivalry; no source treats the relationship as an alliance. Bond - none: pure interest.

UKR.note: The only mortal-enemy grade in Ukraine's map, and the structural one: Russia's aim, as ISW reads the Kremlin's position in February 2026, is neutrality, a limited army and a pro-Russian government in Kyiv; the Atlantic Council argues that Putin cannot accept any deal that secures Ukrainian statehood. Kyiv's reading is on the record: the Rada asked the US to name Russia a state sponsor of terrorism (May 2022) and PACE declared the Russian regime terrorist (Oct 2022). Since January 2026 the two have talked (Abu Dhabi, Geneva, with the US) and the Kremlin has insisted on the Donbas, so 'adversary' is not rhetoric; it describes a war whose settlement would decide whether Ukraine remains a state. Bond - grievance: the open wound is 2014 and 2022, not kinship, whatever Putin says about 'one people'.

relations.summary: All negotiating clusters opened by 2025 and the first three chapters (25, 26, 30) provisionally closed on 14 Jul 2026; the government aims to finish talks by end-2027 and join by 2030, which Commissioner Kos calls realistic if rule-of-law standards hold.

Albania - EU relations

relations.summary: Rama and Vucic jointly ask for Serbia's and Albania's phased entry into the single market and Schengen without a vote, a commissioner or MEPs (FAZ, Feb 2026); the Commission and member states rejected the formula. For Tirana it is a way to get benefits of the Union ahead of full membership and to keep Serbia in the same lane.

sources.title: Serbia and Albania issue joint text on EU accession without veto
Rule-of-law concerns - an obstacle to Albania's EU accession

relations.summary: The Ionian maritime boundary is unresolved. The 2009 delimitation deal was annulled by Albania's Constitutional Court (2010); in Oct 2020 Dendias and Rama agreed to go to the ICJ, but no joint text exists and Greek diplomatic sources say delimitation is no longer an immediate priority (May 2026), contradicting Rama's claim at Delphi.

sources.title: Frozen Courtesies: Albania-Greece relations between rhetoric and reality
Greece, Albania to refer EEZ delimitation to the International Court of Justice

relations.summary: Tirana seeks a personal channel to the Trump administration - the Board of Peace founding seat without the USD 1bn fee (parliament voted 110 of 140 on 22 Jan 2026), Rama in Washington for the 19 Feb inaugural meeting, and the Kushner family's resort concession - against thin economic ties (10% tariff, exports to the US down about 30% in April 2025).

sources.title: Albania, Bulgaria to join Trump's 'Board of Peace'
An initiative by the American President

relations.summary: Candidate country with all clusters open and three chapters provisionally closed (14 Jul 2026); in the Commission's Nov 2025 package Albania was expected to conclude negotiations by end-2027 and the 2025 report found good progress on migration but widespread corruption.

Key findings of the 2025 European Commission report on Albania

relations.summary: Mirrored from XKX's row. Trilateral declaration on military cooperation with Kosovo and Croatia (Tirana, 18 Mar 2025), on training, education and exercises; a declaration of intent, not an alliance treaty. 13 agreements were signed by the two governments on 6 Jul 2023.

sources.title: A Front against Serbia?

relations.summary: First Italy-Albania intergovernmental summit (Rome, Villa Doria Pamphilj, 13 Nov 2025): more than a dozen accords on health, energy, environment, defence industry, education, innovation, diaspora and migration; a business forum planned for the first half of 2026.

Kosovo - bilateral relations

relations.summary: Germany is Kosovo's largest investor and largest bilateral donor, with over EUR 660m in technical and financial cooperation since 1999; the German KFOR contingent is among the Bundeswehr's largest foreign deployments.

sources.title: Kosovo - bilateral relations

relations.summary: Germany supplied 14.0% of Kosovo's imports in August 2025, 15.7% in October and 14.6% in November, the largest single source, and takes 10.7% of exports (November 2025).
relations.note: Monthly Kosovo Agency of Statistics releases as relayed by press; the Federal Foreign Office calls Germany Kosovo's second most important trading partner. No full-year 2025 country breakdown was reached.

sources.title: Exports in Kosovo fall while imports rise
Kosovo - bilateral relations

relations.summary: EU countries account for about 43% of Kosovo's imports and 32% of its exports (Kosovo Customs, as cited by the US Commercial Service); exports to the EU were 34.2% of the total in 2025.
relations.note: Year not stated by the source; February 2025 monthly data gave 44.2% of imports and about 36.5% of exports. The two should be read as a range.

sources.title: Kosovo country commercial guide - market overview

relations.summary: Following the lifting of the 2023 measures, the EU programmes EUR 216m of assistance, of which EUR 205m to be released early in 2026; the Growth Plan funds depend on 13 reforms due by end-June 2026.

sources.title: The EU is lifting all punitive measures
Kosovo - dissolution of parliament

relations.summary: Bilateral trade of about USD 750m, which Erdogan wants above USD 1bn; Kurti's office cites about USD 1bn. Defence industry cooperation is a stated priority.
relations.note: Figures differ between the Turkish presidency (about USD 750m) and Kurti's office (about USD 1bn); the lower, earlier figure is kept.

sources.title: Turkiye ready to support Serbia-Kosovo dialogue process, Erdogan
Prime Minister Kurti received the Minister of Trade of the Republic of Turkey, Bolat
sources.publisher: Office of the Prime Minister of Kosovo

relations.summary: Serbia supplied 3.0% of Kosovo's imports and took 7.7% of its exports in August 2025; Serbian exports to Kosovo fell from about EUR 240m to EUR 75m in June-December 2023 under the Kosovar ban.
relations.note: A single month's data (Kosovo Agency of Statistics via press) and a ban partly lifted in October 2024; the 2026 situation is unverified.

sources.title: Exports in Kosovo fall while imports rise
Kosovo lifts import ban on Serbian goods at Merdare border crossing

relations.summary: Measures imposed on Kosovo by the EU in June 2023 over tensions in the northern municipalities (funds suspended, high-level contacts frozen). The EU announced the lifting on 17 Dec 2025 and the Commission confirmed on 17 Mar 2026 that all had been lifted and all frozen assistance released.

sources.title: Kosovo leaders welcome lifting of all EU punitive measures
The EU is lifting all punitive measures

relations.summary: Banjska attack (24 Sep 2023): armed Serbs killed police sergeant Afrim Bunjaku; three gunmen died. Milan Radoicic, who admitted organising it, lives in Serbia.

sources.title: Kosovo court jails three Serb separatists over 2023 Banjska attack
Kosovo court sentences 3 ethnic Serbs to life, 30 years in prison over 2023 clash

relations.summary: Pristina Basic Court sentenced Blagoje Spasojevic and Vladimir Tolic to life and Dusan Maksimovic to 30 years for Banjska (24 Apr 2026, first instance); the court refused a trial in absentia for Radoicic and 40 others. Serbia called the verdict 'draconian' and 'politically motivated'.

sources.title: Kosovo court hands life sentences over deadly Banjska attack
A first-instance verdict

relations.summary: Ban on Serbian goods introduced in mid-2023; on 7 Oct 2024 eased at the Merdare crossing under inspection, with other crossings staying closed until scanners are installed. EU and US welcomed the decision.

sources.title: Kosovo lifts import ban on Serbian goods at Merdare border crossing
EU, US welcome Kosovo's decision to lift ban on Serbian imports

relations.summary: In the 12 Oct 2025 local elections the Serb List won all four northern municipalities (Zvecan, Leposavic, Zubin Potok, North Mitrovica) and returned to the institutions after 928 days; its vote share fell by 11.4 points on average.

sources.title: Serb List returns to power in north Kosovo after 928 days outside institutions
Serb List dominates local elections but sees decline in support

relations.summary: Kosovo police arrested seven directors of Serbia-run institutions in Gracanica (19 May 2026) and took control of four Serbia-operated railway stations in the north (28 May 2026); in July-September 2026 the judicial councils dismissed 7 prosecutors and 18 judges who sought to return after the 2022 Serb walk-out.

sources.title: Kosovo - October 2026 monthly forecast

relations.summary: NATO announced on 12 Jun 2026 a gradual KFOR reduction toward 3,000-3,500 troops (back to 2023 levels), reversible and coordinated with troop rotations; KFOR will keep supporting the EU-led dialogue.

sources.title: NATO to cut troop numbers in Kosovo amid improved security situation
KFOR Placemat, June 2026

relations.summary: Kosovo imposed its own sanctions on Russia in 2022 (asset freezes, access to markets) and has since aligned with EU packages on Russia and Belarus; Kurti said it had applied 13 packages. Kosovo is not a UN member and takes no UN votes.

sources.title: Kosovo government introduced sanctions on Russia
2025 Commission report on Kosovo - European Parliament resolution

relations.summary: Kosovo announced its first military aid to Ukraine on 20 Mar 2024 (armoured vehicles, trucks and mortar rounds), despite Ukraine not recognising Kosovo; it has also trained Ukrainian deminers.

sources.title: Kosovo announces its first-ever military aid packages for Ukraine

relations.summary: Kosovo's parliament approved on 30 Mar 2026 sending troops to the International Stabilisation Force in Gaza under Trump's Board of Peace (pledge announced in February); the contribution is to be negotiated and approved case by case.

sources.title: Kosovo approves troops to Gaza under US-backed scheme
Kosovo has committed to send Kosovo Security Force members to Gaza

relations.summary: Kosovo announced in July 2023 the purchase of Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones; KFOR said the purchase conflicted with its authority over Kosovo's airspace. Turkey has supported the KSF transformation since 2018 (equipment, training, an ammunition agreement).

sources.title: Kosovo buys Turkish Bayraktar drones
Turkish arming of Kosovo: continuation of military cooperation or Ankara's support for Kurti?

relations.summary: Erdogan received Kurti in a closed-door meeting at the UN General Assembly sidelines in New York on 21 Sep 2026, covering bilateral ties and the region.

sources.title: Turkiye's President meets Kosovar premier at UN sidelines

relations.summary: German Foreign Minister Wadephul visited Pristina on 18 Nov 2025 (Osmani, Kurti, the German KFOR contingent), and met Kurti again in Munich on 14 Feb 2026.

sources.title: Prime Minister Kurti met with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Germany, Wadephul

sources.title: Prime Minister Kurti met with the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Germany, Johann Wadephul
sources.publisher: Office of the Prime Minister of Kosovo

relations.summary: Albanian Prime Minister Rama visited Pristina on 16 Feb 2026 for the first meeting of the new Kurti government; a joint session of the two cabinets, last held in June 2022, is expected but undated.

sources.title: Prime Minister Kurti welcomes Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama
sources.publisher: Office of the Prime Minister of Kosovo

relations.summary: Kurti met Jonathan Powell, the UK Prime Minister's National Security Adviser, at Davos in January 2026; the UK ambassador met him again in February after the new government formed.

sources.title: Prime Minister Kurti met Jonathan Powell, National Security Advisor to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom
sources.publisher: Office of the Prime Minister of Kosovo

sources.title: Prime Minister Kurti receives the Ambassador of the United Kingdom to Kosovo, Jonathan Hargreaves
sources.publisher: Office of the Prime Minister of Kosovo

relations.summary: The Specialist Chambers in The Hague sentenced ex-president Hashim Thaci to 25 years (16 Sep 2026); on 6 Oct 2026 parliament passed, under street protest, a law curbing the court's powers, awaiting the new president's signature.

issues.why: The 2024-25 wave of Western recognitions moved the line that had stood since 1988.

issues.title: Kosovo
issues.subtitle: who recognises it
issues.why: Recognition is Serbia's and Kosovo's whole contest; five EU members still refuse, Belgrade campaigns for withdrawals.

issues.title: Ukraine
issues.subtitle: the last General Assembly vote on the war
issues.why: The February 2026 vote, with the United States abstaining, shows where the coalition stands four years in.

issues.title: Ukraine, March 2022
issues.subtitle: the first vote on the aggression
issues.why: The baseline - 141 in favour - against which every later vote on Ukraine is read.

issues.title: Annexations
